problem: Existing embodied navigation is either indoor or outdoor and depends on priors (precise coordinates, semantic maps, verbose instructions); outdoor point-to-point methods reach only the vicinity of a target and cannot enter through the specific building entrance needed for last-meter delivery.
motivation: Last-mile delivery needs a seamless outdoor-to-indoor transition using only egocentric vision and short instructions like 'go to Starbucks', because precise location and maps are often unavailable or restricted by privacy. The authors observe that the visual cue the agent should attend to changes with distance: target presence when far, signage at mid range, and the entrance when close. No dataset exists for this setting.
key_idea: A vision-centric VLM policy (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) that infers a phase-dependent latent-intention region (signage, then entrance) and is trained to imagine optical-flow-salient regions of the next frame, trained on a new video-synthesis-generated out-to-in dataset.
insight: Learnable query tokens with cross-attention decouple vision-language understanding from trajectory decision-making; removing them nearly destroys performance (SR 0.1m 5.64 vs 33.82). Intention inference matters most for fine-grained success (SR 0.1m 15.24 vs 33.82 without it). Dynamic perception supervision adds a smaller but real gain (SR 0.1m 29.20 vs 33.82), and the ablation keeps the tokens while dropping only the decoding supervision, so the gain is not due to extra parameters.
method: Problem formulation: policy maps the last h=10 RGB frames plus a short instruction to 5 future waypoints, with no GPS or map; the input is a single front-facing camera.

Architecture: ViT image encoder plus learnable language embedding, learnable initial tokens, and Qwen2.5-VL-3B for cross-modal fusion; cross-attention between the tokens and the multimodal content, then a decoder that outputs waypoints.

Latent Intention Inference: stacked transformer blocks plus a regression head predict a bounding box on the sign (mid range) or the door (near); this box guides attention. Stage 1 is supervised with box loss.

Optical-flow-guided dynamic perception: RAFT flow between o_t and o_{t+1}, top-10% flow-magnitude pixel mask; the learnable tokens go through a linear layer plus transposed convolutions to reconstruct only those masked regions of the next frame (L1). The decoder is used only in training.

Vision-instruction alignment flag: negatives built by shuffling instructions and images, BCE loss; the flag signals when the target is not visible so upstream point-to-point navigation or exploration can take over.
Two-stage training: stage 1 trains the intention box (L_bbox). Stage 2 freezes it and trains L_wpts + L_recon + L_flag.

BridgeNavDataset: 55K street-view images; OCR finds shop-sign targets; MoGe-v2 depth builds a 50x50 local occupancy grid; A* gives [x,y,z,yaw] trajectories; Wan2.1-I2V with reprojected point-cloud renderings plus Plücker camera embeddings synthesizes trajectory-consistent videos (100+ h, >10M frames); 20k frames are manually re-annotated with door boxes.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-3B (fine-tuned) with ViT encoder, learnable tokens and waypoint decoder
setting.training_data: BridgeNavDataset: 55K street-view trajectory-instruction pairs, with video synthesized by Wan2.1-I2V (100+ hours, >10M images); 20k manually door-annotated frames for stage 1. The conclusion says 2M pairs, inconsistent with the 55k in the body.
setting.observation: monocular egocentric front-facing RGB (history of 10 frames); no GPS or map
setting.action_space: predicted waypoint sequence [x,y,z,yaw] for the next 5 steps
setting.simulator: none; a generated-video/street-view dataset, with real-world quadruped robot deployment

numbers.extra: Trained on BridgeNavDataset; baselines retrained on the same data with Qwen2.5-VL-3B. TR is trajectory deviation from the A* ground truth (lower is better). The split name is not stated explicitly; 'test' is assumed.

numbers_note: The paper's own benchmark, with its own metrics: SR at 0.1/0.2/0.3 m and trajectory deviation TR. The split is not named. Ablation variants appear in Table 3 (w/o learnable tokens 5.64/42.89/22.39; w/o intention inference 15.24/73.54/14.05; w/o dynamic perception 29.20/86.55/10.69 for SR0.1/SR0.3/TR mean) and are not listed as separate entries.
results: On the new benchmark BridgeNav reaches SR 33.82/70.11/89.55 at 0.1/0.2/0.3 m and mean TR 9.77. The strongest baseline, OmniNav (18.78/46.99/72.39, TR 14.16), is beaten by relative gains of 80.1%, 49.2% and 23.7%, and the mean TR is 31.0% lower. Baselines were retrained on the same data. It also runs on a real quadruped robot at over 5 Hz on an A10 GPU.
limitations: Performs poorly on distorted or very low-resolution images in real-world deployment.
Only tested on quadruped robots, not humanoids; the evaluation is on the authors' own generated dataset and baselines are reproductions, with no real-world quantitative results.
Assumes an upstream point-to-point module brings the agent near the target; the dataset relies on synthesized videos and estimated depth and trajectories.
